epigraph.text: This convergence is a limit as h goes to 0. It does not guarantee a good result for every small h you wish to use.
epigraph.by: Nota Bene 4.3.3 — the whole chapter in one sentence

sections.name: Convergence and Stability of Numerical Methods

cards.q: Derive forward Euler. What single approximation is the whole method?
cards.a:
Taylor expand u(t+h) about t, assuming u ∈ C², and keep two terms:
u(t+h) ≈ u(t) + h·u̇(t) = u(t) + h·f(u(t))
Partition [t₀,T] into n steps of size h with ti = t₀ + ih, start from the known v₀ = u₀, and iterate:
vi+1 = vi + h·f(vi)
That's it — the whole method is ‘truncate the Taylor series after the linear term’. Between grid points you interpolate linearly, which is why an Euler solution is a polygonal path.

Choose [t₀,T] hoping it sits inside the maximal interval of existence — which is what Ch 2 and Ch 3 were for.

r.rot: you're at a point, you know the slope, so walk in that direction for a bit. that's it. that's forward euler. you're pretending the solution is a straight line over each little step, then re-aiming. the error is everything the taylor series had past the linear term, which is why it's only first order and why it drifts.
r.ex: u̇ = au + b, u(0) = 1: v₁ = 1 + h(a+b), v₂ = 1 + 2h(a+b) + h²(a²+ab). You can watch the polynomial in h grow, and compare against the exact (u₀ + b/a)e<sup>at</sup> − b/a.
r.why: Everything else in the chapter is a reaction to Euler's shortcomings. It's also the reason Ch 2's existence theory matters operationally: pick [t₀,T] outside the maximal interval and the method still returns numbers, which approximate nothing.
r.math: v<sub>i+1</sub> = v<sub>i</sub> + hf(v<sub>i</sub>). Explicit: v<sub>i+1</sub> depends only on already-known quantities. LTE is O(h), so first order.

cards.q: Before any stepping happens, set up the discretization. What do you choose, what do you name, and what has to be true of your interval?
cards.a:
Choose a compact interval [t₀, T] that is — hopefully — inside the maximal open interval of existence, and a step h > 0. Take n the largest integer with t₀ + nh ≤ T; assume T = t₀ + nh so it divides evenly.
ti = t₀ + ih,   i = 0, 1, …, n  (4.4)
Keep two sequences straight. ui = u(ti) is the true value, unknown. vi is the computed approximation. Only v₀ = u₀ is known to be exact, straight from the initial condition — every later vi is a guess built on guesses.

The output is the finite list v₀,…,vn, not a function. To get values between nodes you interpolate linearly, which graphically is just connecting (ti, vi) to (ti+1, vi+1) with straight segments.

r.rot: before you can march you need a grid. chop [t₀,T] into n equal steps of size h, label the times t<sub>i</sub>. two letters to keep apart forever: u<sub>i</sub> is the truth (unknown), v<sub>i</sub> is your answer (known, wrong). they agree only at i = 0. the 'hopefully' about the interval of existence is doing real work — a numerical method will happily keep printing numbers past a blowup time.
r.ex: That caveat has teeth: run forward Euler on u̇ = u² past its blowup time and you get finite, plausible, entirely meaningless output. Nothing in the algorithm knows the solution stopped existing.
r.why: It fixes the vocabulary for the whole chapter. Every error definition in §4.2 — local truncation, one-step, global — is some difference between a u and a v, so if those two letters blur, none of the error analysis parses.
r.math: n = ⌊(T − t₀)/h⌋; assume T = t₀ + nh. Output is a sequence, not a function; piecewise-linear interpolation off the nodes.

cards.q: Same method, same h, two IVPs: u̇ = −u + 2 and u̇ = u + 2. Why does the error shrink in one and grow in the other?
cards.a:
Because the dynamics act on the error too. Both panels of Figure 4.1 start from the same exact initial condition, so the initial error is zero; the difference is what the flow does to the errors introduced afterwards.

a = −1 (upper panels): the true solution contracts toward the equilibrium. Errors made at earlier steps are damped by later steps, so the error decreases with t even at fixed h.

a = +1 (lower panels): the true solution expands. Every earlier error is amplified by subsequent steps, so the error increases with t — and the vertical scale goes to 60 rather than 2.

Global error ≠ (number of steps) × (error per step)
The per-step error is roughly the same in both runs. What differs is the accumulation, and that is set by the ODE, not by the method.

Orthogonally, in all cases the approximation improves as h decreases.

r.rot: two separate things decide how wrong you end up. one: how much error each step adds — that's the method, and shrinking h always helps. two: what the system does to errors already on the books — that's the ODE, and you don't get a vote. contracting dynamics forgive your mistakes. expanding dynamics compound them. same solver, same step size, wildly different bills.
r.ex: The log-error plots make it visible: for a = −1 every curve slopes down over time; for a = +1 every curve slopes up. Nothing about forward Euler changed between the two panels.
r.why: It is the reason a chapter on error analysis exists at all. If global error were just per-step error times step count, one theorem would finish the subject — §4.2's recursion and §4.3's stability theory exist precisely to track the amplification factor.
r.math: For u̇ = λu, forward Euler's error recursion carries a factor (1 + hλ) per step. |1 + hλ| < 1 damps, > 1 amplifies — the seed of absolute stability in §4.3.

cards.q: Name the four basic methods and say what distinguishes each.
cards.a:
All four come from choosing where to evaluate f and which difference approximates u̇.
  • Forward Euler: f at the start of the step. Explicit, first order.
  • Backward Euler: f at the end of the step — vi+1 = vi + hf(vi+1). Implicit: vi+1 appears on both sides, so each step needs a solve. First order.
  • Trapezoidal: the average, ½[f(u(t)) + f(u(t+h))]. Implicit, second order.
  • Leapfrog (midpoint): the centered difference [u(t+h) − u(t−h)]/2h. Second order, but needs two previous values.

Explicit methods are cheap per step. Implicit ones cost a solve per step and buy stability, which §4.3 shows is often worth far more.

r.rot: one question: where do you measure the slope? at the start (forward euler, cheap, fragile), at the end (backward euler, costs a solve because you need the answer to compute the answer, but rock solid), or average both (trapezoidal, second order and still stable). leapfrog straddles instead, looking backward and forward. that's the whole design space at this level.
r.ex: Backward Euler on u̇ = λu: v<sub>i+1</sub> = v<sub>i</sub> + hλv<sub>i+1</sub>, so v<sub>i+1</sub> = v<sub>i</sub>/(1−hλ). Here the solve is trivial; for nonlinear f it's a root-find at every step.
r.why: The explicit/implicit split is the central engineering tradeoff in ODE solvers, and it's why `solve_ivp` makes you choose a method. Stiff problems make explicit methods useless no matter how small h is — which §4.3 makes precise.
r.math: Prop 4.2.11: backward Euler is first order; leapfrog is second order.

cards.q: Backward Euler puts the unknown on both sides. What does that cost, and why is Newton's method unusually well behaved here?
cards.a:
vi+1 = vi + hf(vi+1)  (4.8)
vi+1 appears on both sides, so the step is not a formula but an equation to solve. That is what implicit means; forward Euler is explicit because it hands you vi+1 in terms of things you already have.

Sometimes you can solve for vi+1 in closed form. Usually not — so each step runs Newton's method (or a quasi-Newton variant), and every time step now carries the cost of an iterative root-find.

Why Newton thrives: it converges quadratically given a good starting point, and it fails or crawls given a bad one. Here the starting point is free and excellent: vi. If h is small and u is continuous, u(ti) is close to u(ti+1), so you begin the root-find already next to the answer.

The text is blunt that this is worth paying for: there are many circumstances where backward Euler is preferable despite the added per-step complexity. §4.3 says why — stability.

r.rot: forward euler asks 'where does the slope here take me?'. backward euler asks 'what point has a slope that would have landed me exactly there?' — a circular-sounding question you have to solve for. so each step becomes a mini root-finding problem, and you pay for newton iterations. the saving grace: you already have a great guess, namely where you are right now, and newton with a great guess converges absurdly fast.
r.ex: The same self-referential shape appears in the trapezoidal method (4.10), which averages the two Eulers — also implicit, also solved with Newton from v<sub>i</sub>, and usually much more accurate for the same h.
r.why: It sets up the central trade of the chapter: explicit methods are cheap per step but constrained in h; implicit ones cost more per step and buy stability. For stiff problems the implicit method wins outright, because the explicit one needs a step size so small the cheapness is irrelevant.
r.math: Explicit: v<sub>i+1</sub> = F(v<sub>i</sub>). Implicit: G(v<sub>i+1</sub>, v<sub>i</sub>) = 0. Newton is quadratic near the root; v<sub>i</sub> is O(h) away from v<sub>i+1</sub>.

cards.q: What makes a method a finite difference method? Give the recipe and identify the four methods of §4.1 as instances.
cards.a:
Every method of §4.1 is a finite difference method: first uniformly discretize time into t₀,…,tn with ti = t₀ + ih, then compute approximations vi for the true values ui = u(ti). All of them do it the same way:
(i) Approximate u̇(t) by some U̇(t,h) — a finite linear combination of u(t), u(t+h), u(t−h), …

(ii) Approximate f(u(t)) by some F(u(t)). Often F(u) = f(u).
Then impose the relation and solve for u(t+h):
U̇(t,h) ≈ F(u(t))

So a method is just a pair of choices. Examples 4.2.1–4.2.4:

Forward Euler  U̇ = [u(t+h) − u(t)]/h,  F = f(u(t))

Backward Euler  U̇ = [u(t) − u(t−h)]/h,  F = f(u(t))

Trapezoidal  U̇ = [u(t+h) − u(t)]/h,  F = ½[f(u(t)) + f(u(t+h))]

Leapfrog / midpoint  U̇ = [u(t+h) − u(t−h)]/(2h)  (centered),  F = f(u(t))

The two Eulers and the trapezoid differ only in which approximation they change; leapfrog is the one that changes the derivative approximation to a centered difference.

r.rot: every method in the last section is the same template with two blanks filled in. blank one: how do you fake the derivative out of nearby values of u? blank two: how do you fake f(u(t))? set them equal, solve for the next step, done. forward and backward euler use the two obvious one-sided difference quotients and leave f alone. the trapezoid keeps the forward difference but averages f at both ends. leapfrog reaches back two steps and uses a centered difference. that's the whole design space, and where a method's order comes from is which of those approximations you improved.
r.ex: Leapfrog (4.12)–(4.13), vi+1 = vi−1 + 2hf(vi), is fundamentally different from the trapezoidal method: it uses two previous steps to build the next, and it is explicit. That makes it the simplest multistep method — Adams–Bashforth (explicit) and Adams–Moulton (implicit) are the other important ones.
r.why: Naming the two choices separately is what makes the error analysis possible: the LTE is defined as U̇(t,h) − F(u(t)), i.e. exactly the gap in the relation you imposed. So a method's order is a statement about how good those two approximations were together.
r.math: Discretize t<sub>i</sub> = t₀ + ih; choose U̇(t,h) ≈ u̇ and F ≈ f∘u; impose U̇(t,h) ≈ F(u(t)) and solve for v<sub>i+1</sub>.

cards.q: Leapfrog is explicit and second order. What makes that possible, and what new problem does it introduce?
cards.a:
It reaches further back instead of further forward. The centered difference u̇(t) ≈ [u(t+h) − u(t−h)]/2h is second-order accurate by symmetry — the h² terms cancel — and rearranging gives
vi+1 = vi−1 + 2hf(vi)  (4.13)
Fundamentally different from the trapezoidal method, which also gets second order: leapfrog uses two previous steps (vi and vi−1) and stays explicit, while trapezoidal uses one previous step and pays by being implicit.

This is the simplest multistep method. Others named: Adams–Bashforth (explicit) and Adams–Moulton (implicit).

The new problem is the obvious one: v₁ requires v₀ and v−1. A multistep method cannot start itself — you need a one-step method to generate the first values before leapfrog can take over.

r.rot: two ways to buy accuracy. trapezoidal pays with implicitness — solve an equation every step. leapfrog pays with memory — keep the last two values around and straddle the current point. straddling is what kills the error term: a centered difference is symmetric, so the leading error cancels for free. downside, you need two values to get going and at the start you only have one.
r.ex: Proposition 4.2.11 confirms the accounting: backward Euler is first order despite being implicit, and leapfrog is second order despite being explicit. Implicitness buys stability, not accuracy.
r.why: It separates two axes people conflate: explicit-vs-implicit (cost per step, stability) and one-step-vs-multistep (memory, startup, order). Real solvers mix them — and the choice, the text says, depends on the ODE, the precision required, whether you need the whole interval or just the endpoint, and available computing resources.
r.math: Centered difference: [u(t+h) − u(t−h)]/2h = u̇(t) + O(h²), odd terms cancel. Needs v₀ and v₁; bootstrap with a one-step method.

cards.q: Figure 4.2 runs u̇ = −15u + 1 through both Eulers. Describe what happens and what it foreshadows.
cards.a:
The true solution decays fast — rate 15 — toward the equilibrium u = 1/15. Both methods stumble in the first few steps. After that they part company completely.

Forward Euler at larger h oscillates wildly over the entire interval. Not merely inaccurate: it produces qualitatively wrong behaviour, swinging around a solution that is supposed to be settling down.

Backward Euler at the same h gets better over time and converges rapidly to the correct results, even for larger time steps.

Notice that this cannot be an accuracy story. Both methods are first order, so their LTEs are both O(h) — and yet one diverges while the other converges. The distinction has a different name:

forward Euler needs |1 + hλ| ≤ 1; here λ = −15, so h ≤ 2/15 ≈ 0.133
Every h in the figure (0.3, 0.2, 0.1) except the smallest violates it. Backward Euler has no such restriction for decaying λ.

r.rot: the real solution drops to its resting value and stays there. forward euler with too big a step overshoots past it, then overshoots back, harder, forever — it's not slightly wrong, it's doing something the real solution never does. backward euler just slides in and sits down. both methods are equally 'accurate' on paper. accuracy was never the issue.
r.ex: Rate 15 is fast relative to the interval [0,3], so the solution has essentially finished by t = 0.3. Forward Euler's step of h = 0.3 tries to cross the entire transient in one move and lands on the far side.
r.why: It is the whole motivation for §4.3. If accuracy were the only concern, nobody would pay for Newton iterations every step — this figure is the argument that an implicit method can be the only workable choice, and it is the reader's first sight of stiffness.
r.math: Forward Euler on u̇ = λu: v<sub>i+1</sub> = (1 + hλ)v<sub>i</sub>. |1 + hλ| > 1 ⇒ growth; 1 + hλ < −1 ⇒ growth with sign flips, i.e. oscillation. Backward Euler: v<sub>i+1</sub> = v<sub>i</sub>/(1 − hλ), modulus < 1 for all h > 0 when Reλ < 0.

cards.q: Define the three kinds of error, and say why anyone bothers with the two you don't care about.
cards.a:
Definition 4.2.5, starting from the true v₀ = u₀:
  • Global error Ei = vi − ui — how far off you are at step i. This is what you actually want.
  • Local truncation error τ(t) = U̇(t,h) − F(u(t)) — how badly the difference formula approximates the derivative, in one step.
  • One-step error ℒ(t) = v(t+h) − u(t+h) — the error after a single step taken from an exact previous value.

Order p = the largest p with maxi|τi| ∈ O(hp).

Why the other two: the global error is what you want and is much harder to compute. The LTE and one-step error are computable by Taylor's theorem without knowing the true solution — so you bound the thing you can compute and infer the thing you want.

r.rot: three errors, don't mix them up. global = how wrong you are right now after all those steps. that's the one you care about, and the one you can't compute without knowing the answer. LTE = how wrong your slope formula is, per step. one-step = how wrong one step is if you started from the truth. the last two are computable from taylor's theorem alone, which is the whole reason they exist — you bound what you can reach and use it to bound what you can't.
r.ex: Forward Euler has τ<sub>i</sub> = O(h), so it's first order. The trapezoidal method has τ<sub>i</sub> = O(h²), second order. Halve h and Euler's per-step error halves while trapezoid's quarters.
r.why: ‘Order p’ is defined via the LTE, not the global error, and errors accumulate over n = (T−t₀)/h steps — so one power of h gets eaten in going from local to global. That accounting is exactly §4.3.
r.math: Order p ⇔ τ = max|τ<sub>i</sub>| ∈ O(h<sup>p</sup>). Needs f ∈ C<sup>r</sup> for Taylor's theorem to the required order.

cards.q: What three questions about error does §4.2 set out to answer?
cards.a:
Three broad questions about any finite difference method:
(i) Global error bounds. Can we bound how far vi can be from ui, for all i?

(ii) Convergence in h. As h → 0, does the final step vn converge to the correct u(T)? (Remember n grows as h shrinks.)

(iii) Stability in i. For fixed h, does the error |vi − ui| stay bounded as i grows?

These are genuinely different questions. (ii) asks what happens when you refine the grid; (iii) asks what happens when you keep the grid and run longer. A method can pass one and fail the other.

The tool for all three is Taylor's theorem, which is why the section assumes f ∈ Cr for r large enough to expand to whatever order the analysis needs. The overview is given for one-dimensional IVPs, but the principles apply in higher dimensions too.

r.rot: three separate worries, and people run them together. how wrong am i overall — can you bound the damage at every step. does shrinking the step size help — take h to zero and does the answer actually approach the truth. and does it blow up if i keep going — leave h alone, run for a long time, does the error stay bounded or spiral. that last one is stability, and it's the one that bites: a method can converge beautifully as h → 0 and still explode if you run it too long at a step size you chose.
r.ex: Figure 4.2 shows exactly the (iii) failure. On u̇ = −15u + 1 with u₀ = 4, forward Euler oscillates wildly over the whole interval at larger h, while backward Euler gets better over time and converges rapidly even for large steps. Both have some error over the first few steps; they diverge in what happens afterward.
r.why: Keeping (ii) and (iii) apart is the point of the whole section, and it's what §4.3 is named after — Convergence and Stability. The leapfrog method is the cautionary case: second order, perfectly convergent, and unstable for the wrong problem.
r.math: Global bound: sup<sub>i</sub>|E<sub>i</sub>|. Convergence: v<sub>n</sub> → u(T) as h → 0, n = (T−t₀)/h. Stability: |E<sub>i</sub>| bounded as i → ∞ at fixed h.

cards.q: Compute the LTE and the one-step error of forward Euler. How are the two related?
cards.a:
LTE (Example 4.2.6). By definition τ(t) = U̇(t,h) − F(u(t)), and since u̇ = f(u),
|τ(t)| = | [u(t+h) − u(t)]/h − u̇(t) |
Taylor's theorem gives u(t+h) = u(t) + hu̇(t) + (h²/2)ü(t) + O(h³). Substituting, the u(t) cancels and the hu̇(t)/h cancels against −u̇(t), leaving
|τ(t)| ≤ (h/2)|ü(t)| + O(h²) = O(h)
using continuity of ü on the compact [t₀,T]. So forward Euler is a first-order method.

One-step error (Example 4.2.7). Starting from an exact u(t) and taking one step:

ℒ(t) = |u(t+h) − (u(t) + hf(u(t)))| ≤ (h²/2)|ü(t)| + O(h³) = O(h²)
The relation between them is one factor of h:
ℒ(t) = hτ(t) + O(h³)

Which is unsurprising once you look at the definitions — the LTE divides by h and the one-step error does not.

r.rot: expand u(t+h) as a taylor series and watch the cancellation. the constant and the first-order term are exactly what euler's formula reproduces, so they vanish; what's left is the h²/2 ü term. divide by h (that's the LTE) and you get O(h) — first order. don't divide (that's the one-step error) and you get O(h²). so the two errors differ by exactly one factor of h, which is not a coincidence, it's just whether the definition had an h in the denominator. remember which is which and the rest is bookkeeping.
r.ex: The trapezoidal method run through the same machinery (Example 4.2.9) keeps one more Taylor term and lands at |τ(t)| ≤ (h²/12)|u⃗(t)| + O(h³) = O(h²) — second order, and if an implicit method is workable at all it costs little more than backward Euler, which is only first order.
r.why: This is why the LTE is the definition of order rather than the global error: it's computable from Taylor's theorem without knowing the true solution, whereas the global error needs u itself. The whole analysis strategy is to bound what you can reach and then propagate it.
r.math: τ(t) = O(h) ⇒ first order. ℒ(t) = O(h²). ℒ(t) = hτ(t) + O(h³). Needs u ∈ C² on a compact interval.

cards.q: Derive the global error recursion for forward Euler on u̇ = λu. What does the closed form show?
cards.a:
Take the one-dimensional linear IVP u̇(t) = λu(t), u(t₀) = u₀ on [t₀,T]. The LTE at ti is τi = (ui+1 − ui)/h − λui, so the true values satisfy
ui+1 = (1 + λh)ui + hτi
while the approximations satisfy vi+1 = vi + hf(vi) = (1 + λh)vi. Subtracting, with E₀ = v₀ − u₀ = 0:
Ek = (1 + λh)Ek−1 − hτk−1

    = −h ∑i=1k (1 + λh)i τi−1
What it shows. The global error is an accumulation of local truncation errors, each amplified by a power of the growth factor (1 + λh). One step contributes hτ; k steps contribute a weighted sum — and whether that sum stays bounded is entirely a question about |1 + λh|.

The trapezoidal method (Example 4.2.10) gives the same shape with a different amplification factor:

Ek = [(2+λh)/(2−λh)]Ek−1 + [2h/(2−λh)]τk−1
Proposition 4.2.11. Backward Euler is first order; the leapfrog (midpoint) method is second order.

r.rot: the global error isn't just the local errors added up — each one gets multiplied by the growth factor once for every step that follows it. write the recursion out and unroll it and you get a sum of local errors weighted by powers of (1 + λh). that's the whole story of numerical error: you make a small mistake at step 3 and the method keeps multiplying it. if |1 + λh| ≤ 1 the old mistakes shrink and you're fine; if it's bigger than 1 they compound and you get the wild oscillation in figure 4.2. same recursion for the trapezoid with a different factor, and that different factor is why it behaves better.
r.ex: Compare the two amplification factors on a strongly decaying problem (λ very negative). Forward Euler's (1 + λh) leaves the unit disc as soon as h > 2/|λ|, whereas the trapezoid's (2+λh)/(2−λh) has magnitude below 1 for every h > 0. That is exactly the difference between the two panels of Figure 4.2.
r.why: These recursions are stated here and used in §4.3 to derive convergence and stability. That is the payoff of the whole section: convert the computable local quantity into a statement about the global one you actually care about, with the amplification factor carrying all the information.
r.math: u̇ = λu: E<sub>k</sub> = (1+λh)E<sub>k−1</sub> − hτ<sub>k−1</sub> = −h∑<sub>i=1</sub><sup>k</sup>(1+λh)<sup>i</sup>τ<sub>i−1</sub>. Trapezoid factor (2+λh)/(2−λh).

cards.q: Define the order of a method, then show the trapezoidal method is second order. Where does the cancellation happen?
cards.a:
Order p is the largest p with τ = maxi|τi| ∈ O(hp) as h → 0 — it grades the LTE, and bigger p is better.

For the trapezoidal method, expand both sides of τ = [u(t+h) − u(t)]/h − ½[u̇(t) + u̇(t+h)]. The difference quotient gives

u̇(t) + (h/2)ü(t) + (h²/6)u⃛(t) + O(h³)
and the average of the two slopes gives
u̇(t) + (h/2)ü(t) + (h²/4)u⃛(t) + O(h³)
The u̇ terms cancel and — the point — so do the (h/2)ü terms. What survives is (1/6 − 1/4)h²u⃛ = −h²u⃛/12:
|τ(t)| ≤ (h²/12)|u⃛(t)| + O(h³) = O(h²)  (4.27)
Forward Euler's expansion kept its (h/2)ü term — that leftover is its first-order error. Averaging the two endpoint slopes is exactly what annihilates it.

The trade is favourable: backward Euler is also implicit but only first order, so if an implicit method is workable at all, the trapezoidal method doesn't cost much more and gives you an order.

r.rot: forward euler uses the slope at the left end. that's biased — it misses the curvature, and the miss is the h⋅ü term. trapezoidal averages the slope at both ends, and the two biases cancel because one is too low by the same amount the other is too high. what's left is a third-derivative term, one power of h smaller. same implicit machinery as backward euler, one extra order of accuracy, basically free.
r.ex: The cancellation is visible in the fractions: 1/6 from the difference quotient against 1/4 from the average. They don't cancel completely — that's the −1/12 — but the whole h¹ layer above them does.
r.why: Order is the currency for comparing methods, and this shows how orders are actually bought: arrange your approximation so that the next Taylor term cancels. Runge–Kutta in §4.4 is that idea pushed as far as it will go.
r.math: τ ∈ O(h<sup>p</sup>) ⇒ order p. Requires f ∈ C<sup>r</sup> with r large enough for the expansion, and u⃛ bounded on the compact [t₀,T]. Prop 4.2.11: backward Euler p = 1, leapfrog p = 2.

cards.q: Run the global-error derivation for the trapezoidal method on u̇ = λu. Compare the amplification factor to forward Euler's.
cards.a:
Same two-sequence recipe. The LTE is τi = (ui+1 − ui)/h − ½λ(ui+1 + ui); solve for ui+1, and compute vi+1 separately:
ui+1 = [(2 + λh)/(2 − λh)]ui + [2h/(2 − λh)]τi  (4.28)
vi+1 = [(2 + λh)/(2 − λh)]vi  (4.29)
Subtract. E₀ = 0, and for k > 0:
Ek = [(2+λh)/(2−λh)]Ek−1 + [2h/(2−λh)]τk−1  (4.30)
Ek = −[2h/(2−λh)] Σi=1k [(2+λh)/(2−λh)]i τk−i  (4.31)
The shape is identical to forward Euler's (4.26); only the amplification factor changes.
Forward Euler: 1 + λh    Trapezoidal: (2 + λh)/(2 − λh)
For λ < 0 the trapezoidal factor has modulus < 1 for every h > 0, while 1 + λh escapes the unit disk as soon as h > 2/|λ|.

r.rot: every method on u̇ = λu boils down to one number: what each step multiplies your accumulated error by. the derivation is the same three lines every time — write the truth's recursion, write the method's recursion, subtract. forward euler's number is 1 + λh, which leaves the unit disk if h is too big. trapezoidal's is a fraction that stays inside forever when λ < 0. the sum in front is just the pile of per-step errors you're amplifying.
r.ex: (2 + λh)/(2 − λh) is the Cayley-style map: it sends the entire left half plane Re(λh) < 0 into the unit disk, which is why no step restriction appears.
r.why: Two things fall out at once. Global error is per-step error × accumulated amplification, so both order and stability matter and neither substitutes for the other. And the amplification factor computed here is literally the object §4.3 turns into the region of absolute stability.
r.math: Forward Euler stable iff |1 + λh| ≤ 1. Trapezoidal stable iff |2 + λh| ≤ |2 − λh|, i.e. Re(λh) ≤ 0 — the whole left half plane, so A-stable.

cards.q: Define convergence for a finite difference method. Why isn't shrinking h automatically an improvement?
cards.a:
Definition 4.3.1. The method converges on [t₀,T] if vn → u(T) as h → 0, where n = ⌊(T−t₀)/h⌋.

The tension: shrinking h shrinks the LTE and one-step error, but increases the number of steps n = (T−t₀)/h. If the per-step errors don't shrink faster than n grows, shrinking h makes vn worse, not better. Convergence is precisely the claim that the race comes out the right way.

Prop 4.3.2 (forward Euler converges). With τi ≤ Ch and En = −hΣ(1+λh)iτi−1, using 1+x ≤ ex and nh ≤ T−t₀:

|En| ≤ hC·e|λ|(T − t₀) → 0
Note the global error is O(h) while the LTE was O(h) too — the h² per step is multiplied by n ≈ 1/h steps.

r.rot: smaller steps are more accurate per step but you need more of them, and errors pile up. convergence is the claim that accuracy wins that race. and notice what the proof does: it multiplies a per-step error by the number of steps and shows the h's don't fully cancel — you lose exactly one power of h going from local to global. that's why a ‘first-order method’ has O(h) global error from O(h²) steps.
r.ex: The analysis is done on u̇ = λu with λ complex, on purpose: a higher-dimensional linear system decouples into one scalar equation per eigenspace, so the scalar complex case covers it. Nonlinear f is handled through its Lipschitz constant.
r.why: Nota Bene 4.3.3 is the sentence to remember: convergence is a limit as h → 0, and it does not guarantee a good result for the particular small h you chose. That gap is what absolute stability is about.
r.math: Forward Euler: |E<sub>n</sub>| ≤ h²CΣ(1+|λ|h)<sup>i</sup> ≤ h²Cn e<sup>|λ|hn</sup> ≤ hC(T−t₀)e<sup>|λ|</sup>.

cards.q: The whole convergence analysis is done on the scalar IVP u̇ = λu. Why is that not cheating — and why is λ allowed to be complex?
cards.a:
Because a linear system decouples into scalar problems, one per eigenspace. Extension to higher-dimensional linear systems is accomplished by analyzing the scalar ODE that arises in each eigenspace of the full system — and the eigenvalues of a real matrix are routinely complex, so λ must be allowed to range over ℂ from the start.

For nonlinear systems the extension runs through the Lipschitz continuity of f, the same property that powered existence and uniqueness in Ch 2.

Remark 4.3.8 states the practical upgrade: in higher dimensions λ means the eigenvalues of the Jacobian at the current time, and you must choose h so that z = λh lies in the stability region for every eigenvalue simultaneously.

h ≤ min over λ ∈ σ(J) of the constraint imposed by that λ
So the fastest mode dictates h, even if you only care about the slow ones. That is stiffness, stated precisely.

r.rot: one scalar equation looks like a toy, but a linear system is just n of those glued together along eigendirections — so solving the toy solves everything. complex λ isn't exotic, it's what you get the moment a real matrix rotates. and the punchline for real problems: every eigenvalue gets a vote on h, and the most demanding one wins. one fast-decaying mode you don't even care about can force a tiny step size on the whole simulation.
r.ex: Example 3.1.11's oscillator has eigenvalues −1 and −1000. Forward Euler needs h ≤ 2/1000 because of the second one, even though the interesting dynamics live at rate 1 — a 500× penalty for a mode that has already died.
r.why: It is why the one-dimensional analysis in this chapter isn't a simplification for teaching — it is the general theory, via the spectrum. It also explains the entire market for implicit solvers: only a method whose stability region contains the whole left half plane escapes the tyranny of the fastest eigenvalue.
r.math: λ ranges over σ(J(u,t)). Nonlinear extension via the Lipschitz constant of f. Stability condition must hold for all λ at once.

cards.q: Prove forward Euler converges, and explain why global error ends up the same order as the LTE rather than worse.
cards.a:
Prop 4.3.2. Start from the accumulated form (4.26) with |τi| ≤ Ch:
|En| ≤ hΣi=1n|1 + λh|i|τi−1| ≤ h²CΣi=1n(1 + |λ|h)i
Use 1 + x ≤ ex to replace the sum's terms by e|λ|hi, bound each by the largest, and use nh ≤ T − t₀:
|En| ≤ h²Cn⋅e|λ|hn ≤ hC⋅e|λ|(T − t₀)  (4.35)
which → 0 as h → 0.

Track the powers of h and the answer falls out. The LTE is O(h). Each step contributes h⋅τ = O(h²). There are n = O(h−1) steps. One power of h is eaten by the step count, leaving O(h) — the same order as the LTE.

That is the general pattern, and it is the justification for defining a method's order by its LTE at all: the LTE is far easier to compute than the global error, and it usually predicts it. The one-step error, being one order higher than the global error, is an underestimate — intuitively because the global error is roughly the one-step error repeated n = O(h−1) times.

r.rot: each step adds about h² of error. you take 1/h steps. multiply: h. that's the whole accounting. the one-step error looks better than the truth by exactly one power of h because it forgets you have to do it a thousand more times. the e<sup>x</sup> bound is just a convenience for turning a sum of powers into something that doesn't blow up.
r.ex: Prop 4.3.4 runs the identical argument for the trapezoidal method: LTE O(h²), per-step O(h³), times O(h<sup>−1</sup>) steps, global O(h²). Prop 4.3.5 does backward Euler.
r.why: It licenses the entire practice of the field. Nobody computes global error directly — you compute the LTE by Taylor expansion, and this proposition is why that number is the one quoted on the tin.
r.math: 1 + x ≤ e<sup>x</sup> for x > 0; nh ≤ T − t₀. Bound is O(h) and depends on e<sup>|λ|</sup>(T−t₀) — harmless as h → 0, but large for long intervals or fast dynamics.

cards.q: Nota Bene 4.3.3 warns that convergence isn't what you think. What exactly does it not promise?
cards.a:
Convergence is a statement about a limit, not about any particular h. It says vn → u(T) as h → 0. It does not guarantee a good result for every small h you wish to use.

Both properties are needed and neither implies the other:

Convergence: h → 0, with n growing. Stability: h fixed, k → ∞.
Forward Euler on u̇ = −15u + 1 is the demonstration. It converges — Prop 4.3.2 covers every λ ∈ ℂ. And at h = 0.3 it oscillates wildly across the whole interval. Both statements are true at once, because convergence says nothing about behaviour at the h you actually typed in.

This is why §4.3.2 exists at all. Convergence tells you a small enough h works; absolute stability tells you how small.

r.rot: 'it converges' means: keep shrinking h and eventually you'll be fine. it does not mean the h you picked is fine. those are completely different claims and the difference is the whole chapter. convergence is a promise about a limit you never actually reach; stability is a promise about the computation you are actually running.
r.ex: Example 4.3.11 makes the gap numeric: forward Euler on λ = −15 converges, but needs h ≤ 2/15 ≈ 0.133 before the error stops growing exponentially. Between 0.133 and the limit is a whole range of 'small' step sizes that produce garbage.
r.why: It is the standard trap when reading numerical analysis results. An asymptotic statement gives no threshold, and the threshold is exactly what a practitioner needs — which is why absolute stability, a finite computable region, is the usable result.
r.math: Convergence: lim<sub>h→0</sub>|v<sub>n</sub> − u(T)| = 0, n = ⌈(T−t₀)/h⌉. Stability: |E<sub>i</sub>| bounded as i → ∞ at fixed h.

cards.q: Define the region of absolute stability, and give it for forward Euler, backward Euler, trapezoidal, and leapfrog.
cards.a:
For u̇ = λu with step h, write z = λh. The region of absolute stability is the set of z for which the global error does not grow with the step index.
  • Forward Euler: {|1 + z| ≤ 1} — the closed unit disk centred at −1. Small.
  • Backward Euler: {|1 − z| ≥ 1} — everything outside the unit disk centred at +1. Enormous.
  • Trapezoidal: {|(2+z)/(2−z)| ≤ 1} = the entire left half-plane, Re(z) ≤ 0.
  • Leapfrog: only the open segment of the imaginary axis between −i and i.

Higher dimensions (Rmk 4.3.8): λ becomes the eigenvalues of the Jacobian, and h must put z = λh in the region for every eigenvalue.

r.rot: convergence says ‘it works as h → 0.’ stability says ‘does it work at the h you actually used.’ multiply your eigenvalue by your step size, ask whether that point lands in the method's good region. forward euler's region is one small disk, so a stiff problem — one big negative eigenvalue — forces an absurdly tiny h. backward euler's region is basically the whole plane. that's what the extra solve per step buys you.
r.ex: Leapfrog's region is just the imaginary segment, so it's near-useless for real λ — but excellent for skew-symmetric systems (AT = −A), whose eigenvalues are purely imaginary. That's why it survives in Hamiltonian and wave problems.
r.why: This is the concept that decides which solver to reach for. A stiff system has eigenvalues of wildly different magnitudes; the largest one caps h for an explicit method regardless of the accuracy you need. Trapezoidal's whole-left-half-plane region means any h is stable for a decaying system.
r.math: Trapezoidal amplification (2+z)/(2−z); |·| ≤ 1 ⇔ Re(z) ≤ 0. Leapfrog: ξ² = 1 + 2zξ, ξ = z ± √(z²+1), need |ξ| ≤ 1 for both roots.

cards.q: Derive leapfrog's stability region. Why does a second-order explicit method end up nearly useless — and where is it excellent?
cards.a:
Leapfrog's error recursion (4.34) reaches back two steps, so guessing a single ratio won't do. Use the ansatz Ek = ξk in Ek ≈ Ek−2 + 2λhEk−1:
ξ² = 1 + 2zξ,   z = λh  ⇒   ξ = z ± √(z² + 1)
The error is a linear combination of both roots, so you need both to satisfy |ξ| ≤ 1:
Ω = {z ∈ ℂ : |z ± √(z²+1)| ≤ 1}
and that turns out to be just the open segment of the imaginary axis between −i and i. A region with empty interior.

So for real λ — the ordinary one-dimensional case — no h > 0 works at all. Leapfrog is not very useful there.

But for higher-dimensional skew-symmetric systems, AT = −A, the eigenvalues are purely imaginary, landing exactly on the segment. Choose h with |λh| < 1 and leapfrog is stable — explicit, second order, no Newton solve.

r.rot: two-step method, so the error obeys a two-term recursion, so guessing Ek = ξk gives a quadratic — two roots, and both have to behave or the bad one takes over. the region you get is a line segment with no thickness. useless for anything real. but skew-symmetric systems put all their eigenvalues on the imaginary axis, i.e. exactly on that segment, and there leapfrog is a bargain: second-order accuracy with no implicit solve.
r.ex: Skew-symmetric means pure rotation — conservative, energy-preserving dynamics. Leapfrog being the right tool there is why it shows up constantly in molecular dynamics and orbital mechanics under the name Verlet.
r.why: It kills the idea that stability regions are ranked by size. Leapfrog's is vanishingly small yet perfectly matched to an important class of problems, so the question is never 'is this region big' but 'does it contain my λh'.
r.math: Same characteristic-root technique as any linear recurrence. Multistep methods with r steps give a degree-r characteristic polynomial; all roots must lie in the closed unit disk.

cards.q: §4.3.4 is titled Numerical Hogwash. What does the method do, and what is the one hint that it's happening?
cards.a:
Run forward Euler on ẋ = x², x(0) = 1, whose true solution x(t) = 1/(1 − t) blows up at t = 1 and does not exist beyond it. The numerical solution crosses t = 1 with a finite value and continues merrily, for every choice of h.

The text does not soften it: Euler's method (and most other numerical methods) lies to you — pretending it can compute the solution even where none exists at all. And you will normally be running a numerical method because you do not know the true solution, so nothing in the output announces the problem.

The hint: run it at several values of h. For t < 1 the answers agree. For t > 1 they are wildly different and show no sign of settling.

forward Euler converges whenever a solution exists (§4.3.1)
so observed non-convergence in h is evidence, by contraposition, that there is no solution to converge to.

r.rot: the algorithm is a loop. it adds h⋅f(v) to a number, over and over. it has no idea a solution stopped existing, so it keeps printing plausible finite numbers past the blowup and you can plot them and put them in a paper. the only defence: run it at three step sizes. if they agree, believe it. if they diverge from each other, something is wrong — possibly that there's nothing there to compute.
r.ex: Figure 4.5: at h = 1, 0.5, 0.05, 0.01 every curve sails across t = 1 at a different finite height while the true solution has already gone to infinity.
r.why: It is the practical reason the theory in Ch 2 matters to someone who only wants numbers. Existence and the maximal interval aren't formalities — they are the precondition for your output meaning anything, and the solver will not check them for you. Convergence testing across h is the cheap field diagnostic.
r.math: Convergence holds provided a solution exists. Contrapositive: no convergence in h observed ⇒ suspect existence has failed. Necessary, not sufficient.

cards.q: Derive the two-step Adams–Bashforth method. How do you get to choose the coefficients, and what does Adams–Moulton change?
cards.a:
Linear multistep methods are a weighted interpolation over current and past information:
vi+r = vi+r−1 + hΣj=0r bjf(vi+j)  (4.39)
Set br = 0 and the method is explicit: that is Adams–Bashforth. The remaining b0,…,br−1 are then free parameters you spend on accuracy.

For r = 2, Taylor-expand the LTE and group by power of h:

τ(t) = [1 − b₀ − b₁]u̇(t) + h[3/2 − b₁]ü(t) + O(h²)  (4.43)
Kill each bracket in turn. 1 − b₀ − b₁ = 0 and b₁ = 3/2 give b₀ = −½, b₁ = 3/2:
vi+2 = vi+1 + h[−½f(vi) + (3/2)f(vi+1)]  (4.46)
r coefficients bought order r.

Adams–Moulton (Remark 4.3.14): keep br ≠ 0. The method becomes implicit, but that is one more free parameter, so an r-step method reaches order r+1. The one-step Adams–Moulton method is exactly the trapezoidal method.

r.rot: write down the most general method of this shape with unknown weights. taylor expand the error and collect terms by power of h. each coefficient you have is one equation you can force to zero, and each zero kills one order of error. so r free weights buys order r. let the method be implicit and you get one extra weight, hence one extra order — that's the whole difference between bashforth and moulton.
r.ex: The trapezoidal method reappearing as one-step Adams–Moulton is a nice consistency check: it's second order from one step, which is exactly the r+1 the implicit rule predicts.
r.why: It is the general recipe for manufacturing methods rather than memorizing them. You can come up with as many multistep methods as you like at whatever order of accuracy you prefer — accuracy is a linear-algebra problem in the coefficients.
r.math: b<sub>r</sub> = 0 ⇒ explicit, order r. b<sub>r</sub> ≠ 0 ⇒ implicit, order r+1. Coefficients solve a linear system from the Taylor expansion.

cards.q: Multistep methods give high order cheaply. Name the three costs the book lists.
cards.a:
(i) Memory for speed. Each step needs f evaluated at several previous times — but those were already computed, so you store them and each new step costs only one new evaluation of f. Since f can be expensive in high dimensions, that is a real win. The price is spatial complexity: an r-step method stores the previous r−1 evaluations.

(ii) It can't start itself. The IVP gives you u₀ and nothing else, so a 3-step method is missing two values. The fix is to bootstrap — Euler for the first step, 2-step for the second, and so on — which sacrifices accuracy early with no guarantee of making it up. This is 'sort of' ok, and for a quantifiable reason: 2-step Adams–Bashforth has one-step error O(h³) accumulating to O(h²) over T/h steps, while a single forward Euler step contributes O(h²) once. Same order, so the global result stays second order.

(iii) They assume smoothness. The order comes from high-order derivative terms cancelling, which requires the true solution to have those continuous derivatives. For solutions that don't, the cancellation — and the advertised order — simply doesn't happen.

r.rot: three bills. one: you keep old f-values in memory so each step is cheap, but in high dimensions that memory adds up. two: you're missing the first few values and have to fake them with a lower-order method — fine, as long as the startup method is only one order down, because a single O(h²) mistake doesn't wreck an O(h²) answer. three: the accuracy is a taylor-series argument, so if the solution isn't smooth enough, the series argument is void and your fifth-order method is not fifth order.
r.ex: The startup accounting is worth internalizing: an error that happens once may be one order worse than an error that happens every step, and the totals still match. n = O(h−1) is doing the reconciling.
r.why: It's the honest cost sheet for the method class. High order is not free, and the third item is the sneakiest — it fails silently, giving you a low-order answer from a high-order method with no warning, on exactly the non-smooth problems this book takes up later.
r.math: Storage O(r). Startup: bootstrap method may be one order lower. Order p needs u ∈ C<sup>p+1</sup> for the Taylor cancellation.

cards.q: Write the general Runge–Kutta framework. Where in the notation does explicit versus implicit actually live?
cards.a:
A multistage method replaces past data with intermediate evaluations inside the current step:
u(t+h) = u(t) + hΦ(u(t); h),   Φ(u(t); h) = Σi=0q−1 wiki  (4.47–4.48)
Φ is an approximation of f(u(t)) — a weighted blend of slopes sampled at q places. The stages are
ki = f(u(t) + hΣj=0i−1αijkj)  (explicit)
ki = f(u(t) + hΣj=0q−1αijkj)  (implicit)
The whole distinction is the upper limit of the inner sum. Stop at i−1 and ki depends only on stages already computed — evaluate them in order, done. Run to q−1 and every stage depends on every other, so all q stages must be solved for simultaneously.

The simplest RK method is single-stage forward Euler. Implicit RK methods are possible but rarely used, because each evaluation of f is costly in the implicit setting — and there are now q of them tangled together.

r.rot: multistep methods look backwards at old steps. multistage methods look sideways within the current step — poke around at a few intermediate points, average the slopes you find. the entire explicit/implicit distinction is one index in a summation: can stage i see stage i, or only the earlier ones? if it can see itself, you're solving a coupled system every step, q times more painful than backward euler.
r.ex: Read RK4 through this template: q = 4, α₁₀ = α₂₁ = ½, α₃₂ = 1, weights (1, 2, 2, 1)/6. Every α<sub>ij</sub> with j ≥ i is zero, which is what makes it explicit.
r.why: It shows that RK is a family with free parameters, not a formula to memorize. The α and w are yours to spend — on order, on algebraic simplicity, or on stability, which is exactly the choice the SSP methods make.
r.math: q stages, weights w<sub>i</sub>, nodes α<sub>ij</sub>. Explicit ⇔ α<sub>ij</sub> = 0 for j ≥ i (strictly lower triangular Butcher tableau).

cards.q: What is the idea behind Runge–Kutta, and what is the classical fourth-order method?
cards.a:
Spend several evaluations of f inside one step, at cleverly chosen intermediate points, and combine them with weights chosen to cancel low-order Taylor terms. Matching the expansion to second order forces w₀ + w₁ = 1 and w₁α₁₀ = ½ — two equations, three unknowns, so there are infinitely many second-order RK methods.

The classical RK4 (Example 4.4.2):

k₀ = f(u)
k₁ = f(u + (h/2)k₀)
k₂ = f(u + (h/2)k₁)
k₃ = f(u + h·k₂)
u(t+h) ≈ u + (h/6)(k₀ + 2k₁ + 2k₂ + k₃)
Assumes f ∈ C⁵. Popular for decades because the coefficients are memorable and it's easy to implement.

r.rot: euler measures the slope once, at the start, and commits. RK says: take a trial step, look at the slope there, take another trial step, look again — then use a weighted average of all those slopes for the real step. four peeks, weighted 1-2-2-1, and you get fourth-order accuracy. the weights aren't magic, they're just chosen to make the bad taylor terms cancel.
r.ex: Choosing w₀ = w₁ = ½, α₁₀ = 1 in the second-order family gives u + (h/2)[k₀ + k₁] with k₁ = f(u + hk₀) — Heun's method, which is a predictor-corrector: guess with Euler, then average the two slopes.
r.why: RK4 is the default in most solvers, and the tradeoffs are explicit in the text: RK needs little storage and self-starts from a single initial value, but costs several f-evaluations per step, which hurts when f is expensive.
r.math: Second-order conditions: w₀ + w₁ = 1, w₁α₁₀ = ½. RK4 uses 4 stages for order 4; beyond order 4, stages exceed order.

cards.q: Deriving second-order RK needs one calculus identity applied twice. What is it, and why does it make the expansion possible?
cards.a:
The ODE itself, then the chain rule on it:
f(u(t)) = u̇(t)  (4.53)
u̇(t)⋅∂f/∂u = u̇(t)fu(u(t)) = ü(t)  (4.54)
This is what lets you compare the two sides. Taylor-expanding u(t+h) produces derivatives of u; expanding the stages ki = f(u + hαi0f(u)) produces derivatives of f. Without a dictionary between them the two expansions cannot be matched term by term.

With it, the LTE collapses to a sum of brackets:

τ(t) = u̇(t)[1 − w₀ − w₁] + hü(t)[½ − w₁α10] + O(h²)  (4.55)
Set both brackets to zero: w₀ + w₁ = 1 and w₁α10 = ½. Two equations, three unknowns — an infinite family of second-order two-stage methods. Choosing w₀ = w₁ = ½, α10 = 1 is a choice to make things simple, nothing more, and it yields
u(t+h) = u(t) + (h/2)[k₀ + k₁],  k₀ = f(u), k₁ = f(u + hk₀)  (4.56)

r.rot: you have two taylor expansions that speak different languages — one in derivatives of u, one in derivatives of f. u̇ = f and ü = f⋅f<sub>u</sub> is the phrasebook. once everything is in one language you just line up the terms and force each coefficient to vanish. you end up with fewer equations than unknowns, which means an infinite family, which means every RK method you've heard of is just somebody's preferred solution to the same underdetermined system.
r.ex: That (4.56) scheme is Heun's method: take a full Euler step as a trial, evaluate the slope there, then average the two slopes. Structurally the trapezoidal rule, but explicit — the trial step replaces solving for vi+1.
r.why: Underdetermination is the whole story of RK design. Extra freedom is why RK4's coefficients can be chosen to be memorable, and why SSP methods can instead spend that freedom on a bigger stability region.
r.math: Order-2 conditions: Σw<sub>i</sub> = 1 and Σw<sub>i</sub>α<sub>i0</sub> = ½. Higher orders add more conditions faster than they add stages — the reason order 5 needs 6 stages.

cards.q: List the advantages and disadvantages of Runge–Kutta against multistep. Which drawback is easy to miss?
cards.a:
Advantages, both the mirror image of multistep's costs:

(i) Low storage. RK relies only on data at the previous time step, so there is no history buffer.
(ii) Self-starting. It runs from a single initial value — no bootstrap phase, and it can be used to initialize a multistep method.

Disadvantages:
(iii) Several evaluations of f per step. Multistep reuses stored values; RK computes fresh ones every time, which hurts when f is expensive.

(iv) The one that's easy to miss: RK assumes interpolation to an intermediate time is reasonable. Every stage evaluates f somewhere between t and t+h. If the system is nonautonomous and f(u,t) depends on t in a discontinuous way, that assumption is false — interpolating between discrete time steps is not reasonable and can give misleading results.

r.rot: RK and multistep trade the same two resources in opposite directions. multistep: remember old work, cheap steps, awkward startup. RK: forget everything, recompute from scratch, starts instantly. the sneaky failure is (iv) — RK quietly asks f about times between your grid points. if f has a jump there (a switch flips, a controller fires, a forcing turns on), RK evaluates it in a regime that never happens and hands you a confident wrong answer.
r.ex: A forcing term that switches at t = 1: RK4 stepping from 0.8 to 1.2 samples f at 1.0 and 1.2, averaging pre-switch and post-switch behaviour into a single step that describes neither.
r.why: It is a concrete instance of the chapter's recurring theme — every method encodes assumptions about the solution, and it fails silently when they don't hold. Compare multistep's item (iii): high order requires high-order continuous derivatives. Same lesson, different mechanism.
r.math: Disc'ty in t ⇒ the Taylor expansion underlying the order conditions is invalid across the step. Standard remedy: restrict step boundaries to the discontinuity times.

cards.q: Remark 4.4.3 says RK stability regions are easier to derive than multistep ones. Why — and what does the spare freedom buy?
cards.a:
The method is one step, so there is one amplification factor. Substitute f(u) = λu into the algorithm, write out all the terms on a single line, and require the error not to grow. No characteristic polynomial, no multiple roots to control — contrast leapfrog, where Ek = ξk produced a quadratic and both roots had to be tamed.

Where the freedom goes. The order conditions leave coefficients undetermined. Rather than choosing them to be 'nice' and easy to remember, you can choose them to extend the absolute stability region as far into the left half plane as possible. That family is called strong stability preserving (SSP) Runge–Kutta.

A revealing coincidence (Figure 4.6): the stability region of the standard fourth-order RK method coincides exactly with that of the fourth-order Taylor method, which by Prop 4.4.5 is {z : |P₄(z)| ≤ 1} for P₄ the degree-4 Taylor polynomial of ez. Two methods built very differently produce the same amplification polynomial — because for a linear problem, a pth-order one-step method's factor is the degree-p truncation of eλh.

r.rot: one step in, one step out — so plug in λu, grind through the stages, and out pops a single polynomial in z = λh. stable where |that| ≤ 1. no root-chasing. and since the order conditions leave you with leftover knobs, you can turn them toward stability instead of toward memorable fractions. that's SSP. the punchline: RK4 and the 4th-order taylor method land on the exact same region, because on a linear problem any 4th-order one-step method is secretly computing e<sup>z</sup> truncated at degree 4.
r.ex: Prop 4.4.5: as p grows, P<sub>p</sub>(z) approximates e<sup>z</sup> on a larger set, so the region grows toward {|e<sup>z</sup>| ≤ 1} — the left half plane. Figure 4.6's order-10 panel is visibly larger than the order-4 one.
r.why: It reframes method design as optimization. Order is a set of equality constraints; whatever freedom survives is an objective you get to pick, and stability is usually the more valuable objective than tidy coefficients.
r.math: One-step method on u̇ = λu: v<sub>i+1</sub> = R(z)v<sub>i</sub>, z = λh. Order p ⇒ R(z) = e<sup>z</sup> + O(z<sup>p+1</sup>). Stability region {|R(z)| ≤ 1}. Explicit ⇒ R polynomial ⇒ bounded region, never the full half plane.

cards.q: The Taylor-series method is the most obvious high-order scheme imaginable. Why was it unpopular for so long, and what revived it?
cards.a:
The idea. Expand u(t+h) and convert every derivative of u into derivatives of f via u̇ = f and ü = f⋅fu:
vi+1 = vi + hf(vi) + (h²/2)f(vi)fu(vi)  (4.60)
Second order, by construction. Push to order p by including more terms.

The obstacle. You need fu, fuu, and so on, and for a general f those had to be computed symbolically, by hand. Every new problem meant a new symbolic derivation coded up by a human. Example 4.4.4 shows the mess: u̇ = u²cos u needs fu = 2u cos u − u²sin u, and the update already sprawls at second order. Taylor methods were long considered impractical.

The revival: automatic differentiation. fu(vi) can be computed by AD of f at vi, and repeated AD gives higher derivatives. The chain and product rules themselves get automated, so u(k) = dk−1/dtk−1 f(u(t)) is computed entirely algorithmically. That allows schemes of arbitrarily high order p, assuming f ∈ Cp+1, without any symbolic computation.

r.rot: the most honest possible method: just write the taylor series. it needed derivatives of f, and for decades that meant a human doing calculus for every new problem — so nobody used it. automatic differentiation computes exact derivatives from the code for f, no symbols, no finite-difference approximation. suddenly the naive method is the practical one, at any order you want.
r.ex: Third order needs u⃛ = f(f<sub>u</sub>)² + f²f<sub>uu</sub>, which the method approximates as f(v<sub>i</sub>)(f<sub>u</sub>(v<sub>i</sub>))² + f(v<sub>i</sub>)²f<sub>uu</sub>(v<sub>i</sub>) — every piece from repeated AD of the same f.
r.why: It is a case study in how a tooling advance reclassifies a method. Nothing about the mathematics changed; the cost of one operation collapsed, and an abandoned approach became competitive. RK exists in large part because it avoids derivatives of f — its historical advantage.
r.math: Needs f ∈ C<sup>p+1</sup> for order p. AD cost is quadratic in p, which with Prop 4.4.5's error target gives the optimal p = ⌈−½logε + 1⌉.

cards.q: For a Taylor series method, how do you choose the order p, and what happens to stability as p grows?
cards.a:
You choose both h and the order p. Larger p allows a longer step at the same accuracy, but the cost of the Taylor approximation is quadratic in p. Minimizing total flops subject to error below ε gives
p = ⌈ −½ log ε + 1 ⌉
Prop 4.4.5. The region of absolute stability is {z ∈ ℂ : |P(z)| ≤ 1}, where P(z) = Σk=0p zk/k! is the degree-p Taylor polynomial of ez.

The region grows with p — as P(z) approximates ez on a larger set, the stability region approaches the region where |ez| ≤ 1, the left half-plane.

r.rot: higher order lets you take bigger steps, but the per-step cost grows like p², so there's a sweet spot — and it's roughly −½logε, i.e. tighter tolerance wants higher order. bonus: stability improves with p too, because the stability region is where the degree-p taylor polynomial of e<sup>z</sup> stays under 1, and as p grows that set creeps toward the left half plane where the true exponential decays.
r.ex: p = 1 gives |1 + z| ≤ 1, which is exactly forward Euler's disk — forward Euler is the first-order Taylor method. Figure 4.6 shows p = 4 and p = 10 with visibly larger regions.
r.why: It's a rare case where higher order buys accuracy and stability at once, which is not generally true — leapfrog is second order with a nearly empty stability region. It also ties the chapter together: stability regions are always ‘where the amplification factor has modulus ≤ 1’, and each method just has a different amplification factor.
r.math: Ω = {z : |P(z)| ≤ 1}, P = degree-p Taylor polynomial of exp. p = 1 recovers forward Euler.

cards.q: §4.5.1 defines stiff by example. Walk through the lightweight-Bob system and say what the numerical difficulty actually is.
cards.a:
ẏ = Ay,  A = [[0, 1],[−1000, −1001]],  σ(A) = {−1, −1000}
Both eigenvalues are negative, so every solution → 0; the bound ‖x(t)‖ ≤ e−t‖P‖‖P−1‖‖x₀‖ makes the long-run behaviour trivial. Long-term convergence says almost nothing about the short term.

From x₀ = (1,1), x₁ drifts slightly up before turning around, while x₂ plunges — ẋ₂(0) is hugely negative. In phase space the trajectory lurches, then bends sharply, then eases into the origin. That kink is the two eigenvectors:

(−1, 1) for λ = −1  |  (−1/1000, 1) for λ = −1000
The fast eigenspace carries you onto the slow eigenspace; the slow one carries you to the origin.

The numerical bite: after a few thousandths of a second the fast mode is gone — yet an explicit method must keep resolving it forever, because stability demands λh inside the region for every eigenvalue. Forward Euler needs h ≤ 2/1000 across the whole interval [0,4], to track a component that died at t ≈ 0.005. Stiffness is that mismatch: the step size is dictated by the fastest mode, the runtime by the slowest.

r.rot: two decay rates, 1 and 1000. the fast one is over almost immediately — it just slams you onto the slow direction and retires. then you spend four seconds gently drifting to the origin. an explicit solver doesn't care that the fast mode is dead; its stability condition still checks that eigenvalue, so you're stuck taking thousandth-of-a-second steps for four seconds of boring motion. that's stiffness, and it's why you pay for an implicit method.
r.ex: This is Example 3.1.11 reappearing — a very light Bob on a very stiff spring in a viscous fluid. The physical setup is what produces the 1000:1 eigenvalue ratio, and the ill conditioning of A is its algebraic signature.
r.why: It closes the loop on the whole chapter. Figure 4.2, the stability regions, Remark 4.3.8's all-eigenvalues condition and the case for backward Euler all converge here: implicit methods exist because stiff systems are common and explicit methods cannot handle them at any reasonable cost.
r.math: Stiffness ratio |λ<sub>max</sub>|/|λ<sub>min</sub>| = 1000. Explicit: h ≤ 2/|λ<sub>max</sub>| for all t. Implicit with left-half-plane stability: h set by accuracy on the slow mode alone.
